Business plan text:

Wickedgood Candle Return
Wickedgood Candle Return
Executive Summary
Problem
Candles are a popular product, especially as gifts, but when a candle is finished the jar is
usually thrown in the trash. Many candle jars are made of good quality glass that could be used
many more times. Because there is no easy way to send them back, most people either throw them
out or keep a few around the house as storage. This creates unnecessary waste and is a growing
concern for people who care about the environment. At the same time, small candle makers want
to be more sustainable but they are busy making and selling candles. They do not have the time,
space, or money to set up their own system for collecting, cleaning and reusing jars. Customers
who want to do the right thing also have no easy way to see the impact of their choices. We
believe this is a real problem that affects both buyers and sellers of candles.
Solution
Wickedgood Candle Return is a reuse program that makes returning candle jars simple. Our
solution has three parts.
First, a prepaid mailer. A candle maker who partners with us includes a prepaid return mailer
in the box with each candle order, or customers can request one from us. When the candle is
finished the customer puts the empty jar in the mailer and drops it in the mail.
Second, cleaning and refilling. When jars arrive at our workspace we remove leftover wax, wash
and sanitize the glass, inspect it for chips and cracks, and then send good jars back to the
candle maker, who refills them with fresh wax and sells them again.
Third, a data dashboard. Each customer and each candle maker can log in to see how many jars
have been returned, how much glass waste was avoided, and an estimate of the carbon saved. We
think this makes the impact feel real and gives candle makers something to share with their own
customers.
Market
The candle market is large and growing. Candles are sold in grocery stores, gift shops, online
shops and at craft markets. Our focus is on two groups. The first is eco-minded gift buyers,
who often choose products based on values and are willing to pay a bit more for something
sustainable. The second is small and independent candle makers, who number in the thousands
across the country and sell mostly online and at local markets. We estimate that if even a
small share of these makers joined our program, we could handle a very large number of jars
each year. We have not yet done a detailed market sizing, but we believe the growing interest
in sustainability and reuse means demand will continue to increase.
Business Model
We plan to make money in a few ways. Candle makers would pay us a fee for each jar that is
returned, cleaned and sent back to them. Customers may also pay a small fee for the mailer when
it is not included by the candle maker. In the future we could offer premium dashboard features
to candle makers, such as more detailed reports they can use in marketing. We have not
finalized our prices. Our early thinking is that a fee per jar would be lower than the cost of
buying new jars, which would make the program attractive to candle makers, but we still need to
test this. Our costs include the mailers, postage, cleaning supplies, labor and the software
for the dashboard. We expect that as we handle more jars our cost per jar will come down.
Competition
There are other reuse and return programs in the market, and some larger candle brands have

started offering refills for their own products. There are also general packaging reuse
services that work with many kinds of products. What makes us different is that we focus only
on candles and on small makers, and we include a data dashboard so that customers can see their
impact. We believe a focused service is easier for small makers to use than a general one.
Large brands run their own programs and are not likely to serve small makers. We think our
biggest competition is really customers doing nothing, because returning a jar takes effort and
many people will not bother.
Team
Maya Lindqvist is a junior studying environmental science and leads operations and
partnerships. She has experience running a campus recycling drive. Derrick Okonkwo-Hale is a
senior studying industrial design and leads the physical product, including the mailer and the
cleaning process. Priya Venkataraman is a junior studying information systems and builds the
dashboard and handles the data. We are all students at our university and work on this
alongside our classes. We have not yet added any advisors, but we plan to look for mentors with
experience in consumer products and logistics.
Milestones and Financials
So far we have defined our core business concept, built a prototype, and gotten our first
external users. Our prototype includes a basic mailer design, a simple cleaning process we
developed in a shared kitchen space, and a first version of the dashboard. We have had a small
number of friends, family and a few local candle makers try the program, and early feedback has
been positive. People said the idea was interesting and that they liked seeing the dashboard.
We have not yet formed a legal entity and we do not have a website. We have not generated
meaningful revenue. Our spending so far has been small and paid by the founders. In the next
year we hope to form a company, sign up several more candle makers, process a few thousand
jars, and begin charging fees. We expect to reach break-even once we have enough partners, but
we have not built a detailed financial model yet.
What We Are Asking For
We are asking for prize funding from the competition to help us take the next steps. We would
use the money to form a legal entity, build a simple website, buy a larger supply of mailers
and cleaning equipment, and run a pilot with more candle makers. We would also like to receive
mentorship and introductions to people in sustainable consumer products, shipping and small
business. Finally, feedback from the judges would help us improve our plan and decide on our
pricing. We believe Wickedgood Candle Return can make reuse easy for candle lovers and help
small makers be more sustainable, and this competition would help us get started.

Question: Comment on the viability and scalability of the business model and strategy. Address whether the company has a clear path to making money and growing, and evaluate the validity of the entrepreneur's assumptions.

response.text:
The business model and strategy of Wickedgood Candle Return have potential but are not yet fully viable or scalable, with several critical gaps and assumptions that require validation.

**Viability and Scalability:**
- **Revenue Streams:** The model relies on a fee per returned jar and potential premium dashboard features. While the fee structure could be attractive to candle makers (as it may offset the cost of new jars), the assumption that this will be sufficient to cover costs and generate profit is untested. The business lacks a detailed financial model, pricing strategy, and cost structure to validate this.
- **Scalability:** The solution is designed for small candle makers, which is a niche but potentially scalable market. However, the scalability depends heavily on the number of candle makers willing to adopt the program, which is not yet quantified. The business also lacks a clear strategy for expanding beyond the initial target market or entering new regions.
- **Logistics and Operations:** The current operations are limited to a prototype and a shared kitchen. Scaling this to handle thousands of jars annually would require significant investment in logistics, cleaning infrastructure, and labor, which is not addressed in the plan.

**Path to Making Money:**
- The company has a clear idea of how it intends to monetize, but it lacks concrete evidence that the model will be profitable. The assumption that candle makers will pay for the service is not supported by market research or pilot data. The business also needs to address how it will sustain itself once it scales, including the cost of mailers, postage, and cleaning supplies.

**Validity of Assumptions:**
- **Market Demand:** The assumption that eco-conscious consumers and small candle makers will adopt the program is reasonable, but it is not backed by data. The business needs to quantify the size of the target market and demonstrate a clear path to acquisition.
- **Customer Behavior:** The belief that customers will return jars is optimistic. The business must address how it will incentivize participation, given that returning jars requires effort and may not be a priority for all users.
- **Technology and Data Dashboard:** The dashboard is a unique value proposition, but its effectiveness in driving user engagement and providing meaningful impact data is not yet validated. The business needs to test how this feature influences user behavior and retention.

**Conclusion:**
While the business model has a logical structure and a clear mission, it lacks the detailed financial planning, market validation, and operational scalability necessary to be considered viable. The entrepreneurs’ assumptions about customer behavior, pricing, and market size are promising but unproven. To move forward, the company must conduct market research, test pricing models, and develop a detailed financial and operational plan. Without these, the business remains speculative and not yet scalable.
